title: The March Morning a Child Led Lillian Wald to Ludlow Street
dek: In 1893 a nurse followed a little girl to a sick mother in a rear tenement, left medical college and moved to the Lower East Side to nurse its families at home.

story.company: Henry Street Settlement (visiting nursing service, later VNS Health)
story.event: Following a child to her sick mother's tenement on Ludlow Street and deciding to live and nurse on the Lower East Side
story.summary: One March morning in 1893 Lillian Wald, a trained nurse taking courses at the Women's Medical College, was led by a child from her home-nursing class to a sick mother in a rear tenement off Ludlow Street on New York's Lower East Side. She left medical study and, with Mary Brewster, moved into the district to nurse families in their homes, answering calls from families as well as doctors and charging fees only when people could pay. With money from Betty Loeb and Jacob Schiff the work moved to 265 Henry Street in 1895, becoming the Henry Street Settlement and the visiting-nurse service now called VNS Health.
paragraphs: One drizzling March morning in 1893, Lillian Wald was giving a lesson in bed-making to immigrant mothers in an old building on Henry Street, on New York's Lower East Side. She was a trained nurse, then taking courses at the Women's Medical College. A little girl told her that her mother was ill. Wald gathered up the things from the lesson and followed her through Hester and Division streets to the end of Ludlow, across a tenement court and up slimy steps to a rear tenement. A family of seven shared two rooms with boarders, and the mother lay on a bed soiled by a haemorrhage two days old.

The visit, she wrote in 1915, "determined me, within half an hour, to live on the East Side." She called it "a baptism of fire" and never went back to the laboratory or the college. Still awake at dawn, she held what she later called a naive conviction: such conditions lasted because people did not know, and "for me there was a challenge to know and to tell." Her training in nursing, she thought, would give her a real place in the neighbourhood.

Within a day or two Mary Brewster, a friend from training school, agreed to join her. They would live in the district as nurses and take part in its life as citizens. Picturing their own families in the patients' place, they set rules: a nurse's help would not depend on ties to a religious institution or a free dispensary; she would come when families called, not only doctors; and fees would be charged when people could pay, so that care did not feel like charity. After July and August as guests of the College Settlement on Rivington Street, they found a top-floor flat on Jefferson Street before September, the only one their search turned up with a bathtub, and stayed two years.

The work outgrew the flat. Betty Loeb, who had paid for the nursing classes, and her son-in-law, the banker Jacob Schiff, gave Wald the money to move to 265 Henry Street in 1895. By 1905 its nurses worked from 18 district centres and cared for 4,500 patients that year. The visiting-nurse service she began is today VNS Health, which dates its founding to 1893.

quote.text: Take pleasure in one thing and rest in it, in passing from one social act to another social act, thinking of God.
quote.source_title: Thoughts of Marcus Aurelius Antoninus, tr. George Long, Project Gutenberg eBook #15877
quote.connection: Wald's plan began with one sickroom and was carried out one visit at a time. Marcus offers a way to bear work that has no natural end: take pleasure in the single act in front of you, rest in it, and then pass to the next.

reflection: You know what it is to see up close a problem that others only hear described. Wald's first answer was to go and live beside it, and to settle a few plain rules before there was much money: answer when people call, protect their dignity, ask only what they can pay.

In the same chapter she remembers the janitress, Mrs McRae, scolding the two nurses for overdoing themselves and turning visitors away so they could finish a meal or go to bed. Both kinds of rule kept the work going. The second is the one people forget.
invitation: Before the day fills up, name the one call or task that most needs you, and the time you will stop to eat a proper meal. Keep both.

research_notes: The story rests mainly on Wald's own account in The House on Henry Street (1915), Chapters I and II; her feelings and her 'naïve conviction' are given as she wrote them. The book does not print the year beside the March morning, but it places the Jefferson Street move 'before September of the year 1893' after July and August at the College Settlement, captions a photograph of Wald and Brewster 'in hospital uniform, 1893', and the Jewish Women's Archive dates the discovery to 1893, so the story says March 1893. Henry Street's founding date differs: the Jewish Women's Archive says Wald moved to 265 Henry Street in 1895, consistent with Wald's 'two full years' on Jefferson Street from 1893; the National Women's History Museum says Wald and Brewster started the Henry Street Settlement in 1894. The story uses 1895 for the move and does not give a founding year for the settlement as such. Patient figures: the Jewish Women's Archive gives eighteen district centres and 4,500 patients in 1905, and its Women of Valor page says more than 125 families had been visited by January 1894; only the first is used. Wikipedia gives the book's date as 1911, but the Gutenberg edition's front matter says Henry Holt, 1915, which is used. The Henry Street Settlement's own history page and Britannica returned 403 to the verifier and are not cited. The story says 'naive' without the diaeresis Wald used. Wald was born on 10 March 1867, so she was 25 or 26 that March; the story gives no age.
